title: Inner products, orthogonality, orthogonal projections
summary: Lengths, angles and orthogonality in ℝⁿ, orthogonal complements (Row A ⟂ Nul A), and orthogonal projection: the closest point of a subspace to a vector, computed with an orthogonal basis. Projection is the engine behind Gram–Schmidt, least squares and Fourier series.

blocks.text: u·v = uᵀv = u₁v₁ + ⋯ + uₙvₙ. Properties: u·v = v·u; (u + v)·w = u·w + v·w; (cu)·v = c(u·v); u·u ≥ 0 with equality only for u = 0.
‖u‖ = √(u·u). A unit vector has length 1; u/‖u‖ is the unit vector in the direction of u (normalizing). dist(u, v) = ‖u − v‖.
cos θ = (u·v)/(‖u‖‖v‖)
u ⟂ v iff u·v = 0. (The zero vector is orthogonal to everything.)

proof.text: ‖u + v‖² = (u + v)·(u + v) = ‖u‖² + 2u·v + ‖v‖²; the middle term is zero exactly when u·v = 0.

blocks.title: Dot product, lengths, distance, unit vector, angle
blocks.prompt: u = (3, −1, 2), v = (1, 4, −2). Find u·v, ‖u‖, ‖v‖, dist(u, v), the unit vector in the direction of u, and the angle between u and v.

lesson.title: Orthogonal complements and the fundamental subspaces

blocks.text: W⊥ = {z : z·w = 0 for every w ∈ W}. It is a subspace, and W ∩ W⊥ = {0}.

blocks.name: Testing membership
blocks.text: x ∈ W⊥ ⇔ x is orthogonal to every vector in a spanning set of W.

proof.text: If x·wᵢ = 0 for each spanning vector, then x·(Σcᵢwᵢ) = Σcᵢ(x·wᵢ) = 0.

blocks.name: Fundamental subspaces
blocks.text: (Row A)⊥ = Nul A and (Col A)⊥ = Nul Aᵀ. Also dim W + dim W⊥ = n.

proof.text: Ax = 0 says exactly that x dots to zero with every row of A. Apply this to Aᵀ, whose rows are the columns of A, for the second statement. The dimension count is the Rank Theorem: rank + nullity = n.

blocks.title: Find W⊥
items: Write the spanning vectors of W as the ROWS of a matrix.
W⊥ is the null space of that matrix: row reduce and write the parametric vector form.
Check: each basis vector of W⊥ dots to 0 with each spanning vector; dimensions add to n.

blocks.title: W⊥ as a null space
blocks.prompt: W = Span{(1, 0, −1, 2), (0, 1, 1, −1)} ⊆ ℝ⁴. Find a basis of W⊥.
steps: x₁ = x₃ − 2x₄, x₂ = −x₃ + x₄, with x₃, x₄ free.

blocks.title: (Col A)⊥ = Nul Aᵀ
blocks.prompt: A = [1 2; 2 4; 3 6]. Find (Col A)⊥ and check its dimension.
steps: Col A = Span{(1, 2, 3)} (column 2 = 2·column 1), a line in ℝ³.

blocks.text: A set where every pair of distinct vectors is orthogonal. Orthonormal: orthogonal and every vector is a unit vector.

blocks.name: Orthogonal ⇒ independent
blocks.text: An orthogonal set of NONZERO vectors is linearly independent, hence a basis of the subspace it spans.

proof.text: If c₁u₁ + ⋯ + cₚuₚ = 0, dot with uⱼ: every term vanishes except cⱼ(uⱼ·uⱼ), and uⱼ·uⱼ ≠ 0, so cⱼ = 0.

blocks.name: Coordinates in an orthogonal basis
blocks.text: If {u₁, …, uₚ} is an orthogonal basis of W and y ∈ W, then y = c₁u₁ + ⋯ + cₚuₚ with cⱼ = (y·uⱼ)/(uⱼ·uⱼ). No row reduction needed.

proof.text: Dot y = Σcᵢuᵢ with uⱼ; orthogonality leaves y·uⱼ = cⱼuⱼ·uⱼ.

blocks.title: Check orthogonality; coordinates by dot products
blocks.prompt: u₁ = (3, 1, 1), u₂ = (−1, 2, 1), u₃ = (−1/2, −2, 7/2). Show {u₁, u₂, u₃} is an orthogonal basis of ℝ³ and write y = (6, 1, −8) in it.
steps: u₁·u₂ = −3 + 2 + 1 = 0; u₁·u₃ = −3/2 − 2 + 7/2 = 0; u₂·u₃ = 1/2 − 4 + 7/2 = 0. Nonzero and orthogonal ⇒ independent ⇒ basis of ℝ³.

blocks.text: An orthogonal set may contain 0 (then it is dependent). 'Orthogonal basis' excludes 0.

blocks.name: Projection onto a line
blocks.text: For u ≠ 0, the orthogonal projection of y onto L = Span{u} is ŷ = ((y·u)/(u·u))u, and z = y − ŷ is orthogonal to u.

blocks.title: Project onto a line; distance to the line
blocks.prompt: Project y = (7, 6) onto the line through u = (4, 2). Write y as the sum of a vector in the line and a vector orthogonal to it; find the distance from y to the line.

blocks.text: The projection matrix onto Span{u} is P = uuᵀ/(uᵀu). It satisfies P² = P and Pᵀ = P, has rank 1, and its eigenvalues are 1 (on the line) and 0 (on the orthogonal complement). Reflection across the line is 2P − I.
Divide by u·u = ‖u‖², not by ‖u‖.

lesson.title: Orthogonal projection onto a subspace and best approximation

blocks.name: Orthogonal Decomposition Theorem
blocks.text: Let W be a subspace of ℝⁿ. Every y can be written uniquely as y = ŷ + z with ŷ ∈ W and z ∈ W⊥. If {u₁, …, uₚ} is an ORTHOGONAL basis of W, ŷ = projW y = ((y·u₁)/(u₁·u₁))u₁ + ⋯ + ((y·uₚ)/(uₚ·uₚ))uₚ.

proof.text: With ŷ defined by the formula, z = y − ŷ satisfies z·uⱼ = y·uⱼ − ((y·uⱼ)/(uⱼ·uⱼ))uⱼ·uⱼ = 0 (the other terms die by orthogonality), so z ∈ W⊥.
Uniqueness: if ŷ + z = ŷ′ + z′, then ŷ − ŷ′ = z′ − z lies in W ∩ W⊥ = {0}.

blocks.name: Best Approximation Theorem
blocks.text: ŷ = projW y is the closest point of W to y: ‖y − ŷ‖ < ‖y − v‖ for every v ∈ W, v ≠ ŷ. The distance from y to W is ‖y − ŷ‖ = ‖z‖.

proof.text: y − v = (y − ŷ) + (ŷ − v). The first piece is in W⊥, the second in W, so they are orthogonal and Pythagoras gives ‖y − v‖² = ‖y − ŷ‖² + ‖ŷ − v‖² > ‖y − ŷ‖² when v ≠ ŷ.

blocks.text: Why y − ŷ must be orthogonal to all of W: if the error had a component along some direction in W, sliding ŷ in that direction would shorten the error. The closest point is the one where the error has nothing left in W.

blocks.title: Projection onto a plane and distance
blocks.prompt: u₁ = (2, 5, −1), u₂ = (−2, 1, 1), W = Span{u₁, u₂}, y = (1, 2, 3). Find proj_W y, the decomposition y = ŷ + z, and the distance from y to W.

blocks.text: The sum-of-projections formula needs an ORTHOGONAL basis. With a non-orthogonal basis, first apply Gram–Schmidt, or solve the normal equations AᵀAc = Aᵀy and take ŷ = Ac.
If y is already in W, projW y = y. If y ∈ W⊥, the projection is 0.

blocks.name: UᵀU = I
blocks.text: An m×n matrix U has orthonormal columns ⇔ UᵀU = Iₙ. Then ‖Ux‖ = ‖x‖ and (Ux)·(Uy) = x·y: lengths, angles and orthogonality are preserved.

proof.text: Entry (i, j) of UᵀU is uᵢ·uⱼ, which is 1 on the diagonal and 0 off it exactly for an orthonormal set. Then ‖Ux‖² = xᵀUᵀUx = xᵀx.

blocks.name: Projection with orthonormal columns
blocks.text: If the columns of U are an orthonormal basis of W, projW y = UUᵀy. UUᵀ is the projection matrix onto W; it equals I only when U is square.
A SQUARE matrix with orthonormal columns. Then U⁻¹ = Uᵀ, its rows are orthonormal too, and det U = ±1.

blocks.title: Using UᵀU = I
steps: UUᵀ is 3×3 of rank 2 (projection onto the plane Col U), so it is not I₃.
blocks.answer: UᵀU = I₂ and ‖Ux‖ = ‖x‖ = √11; UUᵀ ≠ I (it is the projection onto Col U).

blocks.text: 'Orthogonal matrix' means orthonormal columns AND square. A matrix with merely orthogonal columns satisfies AᵀA = diagonal, so A⁻¹ = diag(1/‖aᵢ‖²)Aᵀ.

blocks.title: True/False on orthogonality
blocks.prompt: (a) If x is orthogonal to every vector in a spanning set of W, then x ∈ W⊥. (b) Every orthogonal set is independent. (c) If U has orthonormal columns, UUᵀ = I. (d) (Row A)⊥ = Nul A. (e) proj_W y depends on which orthogonal basis of W is used. (f) If ‖u + v‖² = ‖u‖² + ‖v‖², then u ⟂ v.
steps: (b) False: {0, e₁} is orthogonal but dependent.
(c) False unless U is square; UUᵀ projects onto Col U.
(e) False: it is the unique closest point.
blocks.answer: (a) T (b) F (c) F (d) T (e) F (f) T

back.text: ŷ = proj_W y is the closest point of W to y: ‖y − ŷ‖ < ‖y − v‖ for every other v ∈ W.

back.text: A vector in both is orthogonal to itself: v·v = 0 ⇒ v = 0. It makes the orthogonal decomposition unique.

items: (a) If ŷ + z = ŷ′ + z′, then ŷ − ŷ′ = z′ − z lies in W ∩ W⊥. A vector v in both satisfies v·v = 0, so v = 0. ∎
det(UᵀU) = det I ⇒ (det U)² = 1 ⇒ det U = ±1. ∎
